claim: The IL-6/JAK/STAT signaling pathway is positively enriched in human tendinopathic tendons compared to normal control tendons.
source: GSEA revealed a positive enrichment of the IL-6/JAK/STAT pathway (q-value: 0.003) alongside gene sets matching well-known tendinopathy hallmarks such as neo-vascularization (i.e. angiogenesis, mTORC1 signaling) and hypercellularity (i.e. G2M checkpoint, mitotic spindle, MYC targets v1, epithelial mesenchymal transition, and E2F targets) in the tendinopathic samples compared to the normal controls (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of microarray data showing q-value of 0.003, and visualized in Figure 1C and D showing enrichment scores and GSEA plots.

claim: IL6 transcript expression is significantly upregulated in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 1.529 and p-value of 0.021.
source: Further analysis revealed significantly upregulated IL6 and IL6 signaling transducer (IL6ST, also known as GP130) transcripts in tendinopathic tendon tissue (Figure 1A and B, Table 1).
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis with statistical significance testing, shown in volcano plot (Figure 1A) and Table 1.

claim: IL6ST (GP130) transcript expression is significantly upregulated in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 0.399 and p-value of 0.035.
source: Further analysis revealed significantly upregulated IL6 and IL6 signaling transducer (IL6ST, also known as GP130) transcripts in tendinopathic tendon tissue (Figure 1A and B, Table 1).
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis with statistical significance testing, shown in Table 1.

claim: IL6RA (IL-6 receptor) expression trends toward downregulation in human tendinopathic tendons.
source: Conversely, IL6 receptor (IL6RA) expression trended toward downregulation.
evidence: Based on microarray analysis showing effect size of -0.423 with p-value of 0.116 (Table 1), indicating a trend but not reaching statistical significance.

claim: ADAM10 transcript expression is significantly upregulated in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 0.606 and p-value of 0.023.
source: Focusing on proteases that generate soluble IL6RA, we found significant upregulation of both ADAM10 and ADAM17 in human tendinopathic tendons.
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: ADAM17 transcript expression is significantly upregulated in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 0.541 and p-value of 0.014.
source: Focusing on proteases that generate soluble IL6RA, we found significant upregulation of both ADAM10 and ADAM17 in human tendinopathic tendons.
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: STAT3 transcript expression is significantly upregulated in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 0.36 and p-value of 0.036.
source: Downstream of IL6 receptor binding, JAK1 trended toward upregulation and STAT3 was upregulated significantly.
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Interleukin-11 (IL11) transcript expression is significantly upregulated in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 0.913 and p-value of 0.048.
source: Aside from IL6, another significantly upregulated member of the IL-6 family was interleukin-11 (IL11).
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: COL1A1 transcript expression is significantly increased in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 0.523 and p-value of 0.04.
source: In line with aberrant matrix turnover generally featured in tendinopathy, the transcripts of the following genes were significantly increased in the tendinopathic samples: COL1A1, COL1A2, COL18A1.
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: COL1A2 transcript expression is significantly increased in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 0.624 and p-value of 0.013.
source: In line with aberrant matrix turnover generally featured in tendinopathy, the transcripts of the following genes were significantly increased in the tendinopathic samples: COL1A1, COL1A2, COL18A1.
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: COL18A1 transcript expression is significantly increased in human tendinopathic tendons with an effect size of 1.112 and p-value of 0.009.
source: In line with aberrant matrix turnover generally featured in tendinopathy, the transcripts of the following genes were significantly increased in the tendinopathic samples: COL1A1, COL1A2, COL18A1.
evidence: Directly measured from microarray data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Gene sets related to angiogenesis are positively enriched in human tendinopathic tendons.
source: GSEA revealed a positive enrichment of the IL-6/JAK/STAT pathway (q-value: 0.003) alongside gene sets matching well-known tendinopathy hallmarks such as neo-vascularization (i.e. angiogenesis, mTORC1 signaling) and hypercellularity (i.e. G2M checkpoint, mitotic spindle, MYC targets v1, epithelial mesenchymal transition, and E2F targets) in the tendinopathic samples compared to the normal controls (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gene sets related to hypercellularity including G2M checkpoint, mitotic spindle, MYC targets v1, epithelial mesenchymal transition, and E2F targets are positively enriched in human tendinopathic tendons.
source: GSEA revealed a positive enrichment of the IL-6/JAK/STAT pathway (q-value: 0.003) alongside gene sets matching well-known tendinopathy hallmarks such as neo-vascularization (i.e. angiogenesis, mTORC1 signaling) and hypercellularity (i.e. G2M checkpoint, mitotic spindle, MYC targets v1, epithelial mesenchymal transition, and E2F targets) in the tendinopathic samples compared to the normal controls (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Biological processes related to wound healing are enriched in human tendinopathic tendons.
source: We then looked further into aberrant biological processes by mapping the significantly changed single transcripts (p-value<0.01) to the respective gene ontology (GO) database in an overrepresentation analysis (ORA) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The emerging processes pointed toward ongoing morphogenesis and wound healing favoring hypercellularity (i.e. proliferation, migration) and ECM turnover, which are both established hallmarks of tendinopathy.
evidence: Supported by GO overrepresentation analysis shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: Signature gene sets of several fibroblast populations are significantly enriched in human tendinopathic tendons.
source: Lastly, we matched the detected transcript changes to the human cell-type signature gene sets from MSigDB in a GSEA to estimate the contribution of fibroblasts to the aberrant processes (Subramanian et al., 2005; Liberzon et al., 2015). While this database does not yet include tendon-specific fibroblast populations, the signature gene sets of several fibroblast populations were significantly enriched by the transcript changes detected in tendinopathic tendons (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of cell-type signature gene sets shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The percentage of IL-6+ cells is slightly increased in human tendinopathic tendons compared to normal control tendons.
source: The percentage of IL-6 secreting cells was only slightly increased in tendinopathic compared to healthy control tendons (Table 2).
evidence: Based on quantification of immunofluorescence microscopy images showing median of 33.3% in tendinopathic vs 22.5% in normal control (Table 2).

claim: The percentage of CD90+ cells is significantly increased in human tendinopathic tendons (median 45.6%) compared to normal control tendons (median 4.3%).
source: The subsequent spatial proximity-based quantification confirmed this initial visual impression by detecting a statistically significant difference in the percentage CD90+ in the normal control compared to the tendinopathic tendon (Table 2).
evidence: Based on quantification of immunofluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2C and Table 2, with statistical testing.

claim: The percentage of IL-6R+ cells is significantly increased in human tendinopathic tendons (median 37.5%) compared to normal control tendons (median 5.3%).
source: We could confirm this again with spatial proximity-based quantification detecting a statistically significant difference in the percentage of IL-6R+ cells in normal control compared to tendinopathic tendons (Table 2).
evidence: Based on quantification of immunofluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2D and Table 2, with statistical testing.

claim: In human tendinopathic tendons, a significantly higher percentage of IL-6+ cells are CD90+ (median 50.2%) rather than CD68+ (median 5.02%).
source: Indeed, quantification of the spatial signal overlay showed a significantly higher percentage of cells in spatial proximity to IL-6 to be CD90+ rather than CD68+ cells (Table 3).
evidence: Based on co-localization analysis of immunofluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 3B and Table 3, with statistical testing.

claim: In human tendinopathic tendons, a significantly higher percentage of IL-6R+ cells are CD90+ (median 95.0%) rather than CD68+ (median 37.0%).
source: Quantifying the difference based on spatial proximity confirmed this impression (Table 3) and the statistical analysis judged it to be statistically significant.
evidence: Based on co-localization analysis of immunofluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 3C and Table 3, with statistical testing.

claim: IL-6 is present in the supernatant of wildtype core explants but not in the supernatant of extrinsic fibroblasts cultured in collagen hydrogel.
source: Both were present in the supernatant (IL-6) and on CD45+ cell populations (IL-6R) from core explants, but not in the supernatant or on the surface of extrinsic fibroblasts cultured in a collagen hydrogel.
evidence: Based on secretome analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: IL-6R is present on CD45+ cell populations from core explants but not on the surface of extrinsic fibroblasts.
source: Both were present in the supernatant (IL-6) and on CD45+ cell populations (IL-6R) from core explants, but not in the supernatant or on the surface of extrinsic fibroblasts cultured in a collagen hydrogel.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Integration of an IL-6 KO core increased transcripts of 256 genes and decreased transcripts of 98 genes in the surrounding extrinsic fibroblast compartment compared to WT core.
source: Overall, integration of an IL-6 KO core increased transcripts of 256 genes in the surrounding extrinsic compartment, decreased transcripts of 98 genes, and left 15,295 unchanged (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Based on bulk RNA-seq analysis of extrinsic fibroblasts after 7 days of co-culture, shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Out of 195 significantly enriched biological processes in the extrinsic compartment of KO core assembloids, 10 (5.1%) are linked to changes in local cellularity and another 10 to ECM turnover.
source: Out of the 195 significantly enriched biological processes (adjusted p-value<0.05) in the extrinsic compartment of KO core // fibroblast assembloids, 10 (5.1%) could be linked to changes in local cellularity and another 10 to ECM turnover (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on GO overrepresentation analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: IL-6 signaling by the core correlates positively with processes aimed at increasing cellularity and ECM turnover in extrinsic fibroblasts.
source: When stratifying the respective contribution of transcripts increased and decreased around a KO core compared to a WT core to the top 20 enriched GO biological processes and significantly enriched MSigDB mouse hallmarks, we found that IL-6 signaling by the core correlated positively with processes aimed at increasing cellularity and ECM turnover (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D), which are both hallmarks of tendinopathic tissues and indicators of an activated tissue state.
evidence: Based on directional analysis of GO and GSEA enrichment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Total cell number is significantly higher in WT core assembloids compared to KO core assembloids.
source: We went on to confirm these visual impressions using quantitative methods, finding a significantly increased total cell number in assembloids with a WT core compared to those with a KO core (Figure 6B, Table 4).
evidence: Based on quantification of fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6B and Table 4, with statistical testing showing p<0.01.

claim: The ratio between core-resident and extrinsic ScxGFP fibroblasts is significantly higher in WT core assembloids compared to KO core assembloids.
source: The WT core // ScxGFP fibroblast assembloids exhibited the highest core-resident to extrinsic ScxGFP fibroblast ratio and KO core // ScxGFP fibroblast assembloids had a significantly lower core-resident to extrinsic ScxGFP fibroblast ratio.
evidence: Based on spatial distribution analysis of ScxGFP cells shown in Figure 6D and Table 4, with statistical testing showing p<0.01.

claim: Tocilizumab treatment significantly decreases the number of ScxGFP cells in WT core assembloids.
source: In alignment with the previous results and the hypothesis, IL-6 desensitization decreased the total cell number in trend (Figure 6B, Table 4), the ScxGFP cell number significantly (Figure 6C, Table 4), and the ratio between core-resident and extrinsic ScxGFP fibroblasts significantly as well (Figure 6D, Table 4).
evidence: Based on quantification of fluorescence microscopy images after tocilizumab treatment shown in Figure 6C and Table 4, with statistical testing showing p<0.05.

claim: Addition of recombinant IL-6 to KO core assembloids significantly increases the total cell number and the number of ScxGFP cells.
source: The addition of recombinant IL-6 to KO core // fibroblast assembloids significantly increased the total cell number and the number of ScxGFP cells, rescuing the WT phenotype of IL-6 enhanced cell proliferation in the extrinsic compartment.
evidence: Based on quantification of fluorescence microscopy images after recombinant IL-6 treatment shown in Figure 6B-C and Table 4, with statistical testing showing p<0.01.

claim: Addition of recombinant IL-6 to KO core assembloids does not rescue core-directed migration of ScxGFP cells.
source: However, core-directed migration was not rescued by recombinant IL-6.
evidence: Based on spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 6D-E and Table 4.

claim: No observable trends or statistically detectable differences in ScxGFP cell distribution were detected between IL-6 WT and IL-6 KO mice 14 days after Achilles tenotomy.
source: No observable trends or statistically detectable differences in the highly variable and complex ScxGFP cell migration patterns were detected between IL-6 WT and IL-6 KO mice (Figure 7B, left and right).
evidence: Based on analysis of fluorescence microscopy images from in vivo tenotomy model shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Exposing WT core explants to fibroblasts for 7 days increased 446 transcripts and decreased 217 transcripts compared to cell-free controls.
source: Exposing WT core explants to fibroblasts (WT core // fibroblasts) for 7 days increased 446 transcripts, decreased 217 transcripts, and left 19,694 transcripts unchanged (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Based on bulk RNA-seq analysis of core explants shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: Transcripts for Col3a1, Col1a1, Mmp13, Mmp3, and Mmp9 are increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts.
source: Indeed, transcripts for Col3a1, Col1a1, Mmp13, Mmp3, and Mmp9 were increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts (Figure 8, Table 5).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 8 and Table 5, with specific effect sizes and p-values provided.

claim: Col3a1 transcript expression is significantly increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts with an effect size of 1.1 and p-value of 8.40E-11.
source: Indeed, transcripts for Col3a1, Col1a1, Mmp13, Mmp3, and Mmp9 were increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts (Figure 8, Table 5).
evidence: Directly measured from RNA-seq data shown in Table 5.

claim: Mmp13 transcript expression is significantly increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts with an effect size of 0.91 and p-value of 1.20E-06.
source: Indeed, transcripts for Col3a1, Col1a1, Mmp13, Mmp3, and Mmp9 were increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts (Figure 8, Table 5).
evidence: Directly measured from RNA-seq data shown in Table 5.

claim: Mmp3 transcript expression is significantly increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts with an effect size of 0.64 and p-value of 0.0006.
source: Indeed, transcripts for Col3a1, Col1a1, Mmp13, Mmp3, and Mmp9 were increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts (Figure 8, Table 5).
evidence: Directly measured from RNA-seq data shown in Table 5.

claim: Scx transcript expression is significantly increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts with an effect size of 0.98 and p-value of 0.00006.
source: In line with the previous paragraphs reporting fibroblast migration in vitro, some of the increased transcripts (i.e. Scx and Sox9) indicated an enrichment of Scx+ and/or Sox9+ fibroblasts in the WT core explants of WT core // fibroblast assembloids compared to those of WT core // cell-free assembloids.
evidence: Directly measured from RNA-seq data shown in Table 5.

claim: Sox9 transcript expression is significantly increased in core explants co-cultured with fibroblasts with an effect size of 0.6 and p-value of 0.001.
source: In line with the previous paragraphs reporting fibroblast migration in vitro, some of the increased transcripts (i.e. Scx and Sox9) indicated an enrichment of Scx+ and/or Sox9+ fibroblasts in the WT core explants of WT core // fibroblast assembloids compared to those of WT core // cell-free assembloids.
evidence: Directly measured from RNA-seq data shown in Table 5.

claim: An IL-6 KO in core explants results in 276 upregulated and 192 downregulated genes compared to WT core explants when co-cultured with fibroblasts.
source: On the transcript level, we found 276 upregulated, 192 downregulated, and 20,204 unchanged genes in the core of KO core // fibroblast assembloids compared to that of WT core // fibroblast assembloids (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: Based on bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: About a third of all biological process signatures enriched by the presence of fibroblasts are also enriched by the IL-6 KO in core explants.
source: Overall, about a third of all signatures enriched by the presence of fibroblasts were also enriched by the IL-6 KO (Figure 9E).
evidence: Based on Venn diagram analysis of GO enrichment overlaps shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The linear elastic modulus decreases most strongly in WT core assembloids with fibroblasts between day 0 and day 21.
source: In WT core // fibroblast assembloids, the linear elastic modulus decreased the most between the initial clamping of the core explant and 21 days of co-culture (light blue).
evidence: Based on mechanical testing shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The linear elastic modulus of KO core assembloids and devitalized WT core assembloids decreases less than WT core assembloids with fibroblasts.
source: The linear elastic modulus of assembloids containing a KO core (violet) or a WT core explant devitalized through multiple freeze-thaw cycles (black) decreased as well, but not as fast or as strongly.
evidence: Based on mechanical testing shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Tendinopathies represent approximately 22% of all sport-related injuries.
source: Tendinopathies represent the largest group of common tendon diseases and approximately 22% of all sport-related injuries (Florit et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Florit et al., 2019.

claim: Chronic tendon lesions underlying tendinopathies feature accelerated extracellular matrix turnover and proliferation of reparative fibroblast populations.
source: These chronic tendon lesions underlying tendinopathies feature characteristics of normal wound healing including accelerated extracellular matrix (ECM) turnover and proliferation of reparative fibroblast populations as well as their migration to replace and repopulate damaged tissues (Howell et al., 2017; Li et al., 2007; Millar et al., 2021; Gelberman et al., 1986; Sharma and Maffulli, 2006; Harvey et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: In tendon, reparative fibroblast populations are assumed to reside primarily in the extrinsic compartment comprising epitenon and paratenon.
source: In tendon, reparative (e.g. Scx+) fibroblast populations are assumed to reside primarily in the extrinsic compartment comprising epitenon and paratenon from where they are recruited to the damaged intrinsic compartment embodied by the load-bearing tendon core (Gelberman et al., 1986; Dyment et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2021; Mendias et al., 2012; Mienaltowski et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: IL-6 activates and recruits satellite cells in muscle and dermal fibroblasts in skin.
source: Satellite cells in muscle and dermal fibroblasts in skin are activated and recruited by interleukin-6 (IL-6), a key player in the acute phase response to stress (Serrano et al., 2008; Ceafalan et al., 2014; Muñoz-Cánoves et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Serrano et al., 2008; Ceafalan et al., 2014; Muñoz-Cánoves et al., 2013.

claim: IL-6 transmits its signal via classical or trans-signaling in humans.
source: In humans, IL-6 transmits its signal via classical or trans-signaling (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Su et al., 2017.

claim: Classical IL-6 signaling involves the membrane-bound receptor IL-6R forming a homodimer with gp130 upon IL-6 binding.
source: Classical signaling involves the membrane-bound receptor IL-6R, which forms a homodimer with gp130 upon IL-6 binding.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IL-6 signaling mechanisms.

claim: Trans-signaling involves solubilized IL-6R (sIL-6R) that has been cleaved from the cell membrane by metalloproteases, mostly ADAM10 and ADAM17.
source: Trans-signaling works similarly, except that the IL-6R has been solubilized (sIL-6R) by metalloproteases (mostly ADAM10 and 17) (Villar-Fincheira et al., 2021), which cleave it from the cell membrane (Su et al., 2017; Villar-Fincheira et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Su et al., 2017 and Villar-Fincheira et al., 2021.

claim: IL-6 signal transduction runs via two major pathways: JAK/STAT/ERK and SHP2/GAB2/MAPK.
source: Regardless of classical or trans-signaling initiation, further transduction of the IL-6 signal runs via two major pathways (JAK/STAT/ERK [Zhang et al., 2013; Watanabe et al., 2004] and SHP2/GAB2/MAPK [Ernst and Jenkins, 2004; Eulenfeld et al., 2012]) to turn on cellular processes inducing proliferation, migration, metabolic adaptations, and tissue turnover (Su et al., 2017; Choy and Rose-John, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: In chronic muscle lesions like Duchenne muscular dystrophy, IL-6 is persistently upregulated.
source: In chronic muscle lesions like Duchenne muscular dystrophy, IL-6 is persistently upregulated, and anti-IL-6 receptor antibodies have been proposed as treatment options (Wada et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wada et al., 2017.

claim: Anti-IL-6 receptor antibodies like tocilizumab are routinely used in chronic inflammatory diseases like systemic sclerosis, psoriasis, and rheumatoid arthritis.
source: Anti-IL-6 receptor antibodies (IL-6 inhibitors) like tocilizumab inhibit both classical and trans-signaling and are routinely used in other chronic inflammatory diseases like systemic sclerosis, psoriasis, and rheumatoid arthritis (Tanaka et al., 2014; Choy et al., 2020; Srirangan and Choy, 2010; Lewinson et al., 2018; Simone et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: IL-6 inhibitors have been shown to reduce arthritis-concomitant tendon inflammation.
source: In this context, IL-6 inhibitors have been shown to reduce disease hallmarks including arthritis-concomitant tendon inflammation (Poutoglidou et al., 2021; Choy et al., 2002; Emery et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poutoglidou et al., 2021; Choy et al., 2002; Emery et al., 2008.

claim: Histological and molecular characteristics of tendinopathy include hypercellularity, disorganized collagen fibers including mechanically inferior collagen-3, and dysregulated ECM homeostasis.
source: Histological and molecular characteristics of tendinopathy include hypercellularity, disorganized collagen fibers including mechanically inferior collagen-3, and dysregulated ECM homeostasis (Millar et al., 2021; Andersson et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2006; Riley et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: CD90 is a common marker of reparative fibroblasts.
source: The cell surface protein CD90 is a common marker of reparative fibroblasts (Ho et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ho et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2021.

claim: The microarray dataset analyzed contained samples from 23 normal and 23 tendinopathic human tendons of mixed anatomical origin, with 5 normal and 5 tendinopathic samples from sheathed tendons excluded.
source: To deduce common disease patterns affecting tendons from diverse anatomical locations, the microarray dataset contained analyzed samples from 23 normal and 23 tendinopathic human tendons of mixed anatomical origin. We excluded 5 normal and 5 tendinopathic samples from sheathed tendons originally included in the dataset, as those tendons are organized into different sub-compartments than the non-sheathed tendons remaining in the dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of dataset composition and filtering criteria.

claim: 240 genes were significantly upregulated and 474 genes were significantly downregulated in tendinopathic compared to normal control tendons.
source: Overall, we found 240 significantly upregulated genes, 474 significantly downregulated genes, and 20,359 not-differentially regulated genes in tendinopathic compared to normal control tendons.
evidence: Based on differential expression analysis of microarray data.

claim: IL-6 in normal control tendons appears to be confined to the extrinsic compartment.
source: In normal control tendons, the fluorescent signal stemming from the IL-6 antibody (Figure 2B, left side, red) appeared to be confined to the extrinsic compartment, which we identified based on the clustering of cells with a roundish nucleus (blue).
evidence: Based on visual observation of immunofluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In tendinopathic tendons, IL-6 signal is more evenly distributed over the tissue section and tendon compartments compared to normal control.
source: In tendinopathic tendons (Figure 2B, right side), it was challenging to identify the extrinsic compartment due to the characteristic change in cell shape from elongated to more roundish in both the extrinsic compartment and the load-bearing core tissue. While the signal of the IL-6 antibody was more evenly distributed over the tendinopathic tissue section and tendon compartments compared to the control, it was still more prominent around roundish than elongated cells.
evidence: Based on visual observation and quantification of immunofluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The downregulation of IL6RA transcript in tendinopathic tendons could indicate increased trans-signaling aimed at stromal cells unable to express IL6RA.
source: While analysis of human samples indicated the expression of IL6, IL6ST, and ADAM10 (known to transform membrane-bound IL-6R into soluble IL-6R) to be upregulated in tendinopathic tendons, the expression of IL6RA itself was downregulated. We speculate that this points toward increased trans-signaling aimed at stromal cells unable to express IL6RA, in this tendinopathic context particularly the stromal fibroblasts and fibroblast-like cell populations indicated to be enriched by the cell-type signatures (Nowell et al., 2003; Rose-John, 2012).
evidence: Based on inference from transcript expression patterns and known IL-6 signaling mechanisms, with supporting citations.

claim: The mismatch between IL6RA transcript downregulation and IL-6R protein upregulation in tendinopathic tendons could be a legacy from earlier disease stages.
source: In contrast to the relative transcript-level decrease of IL6RA in tendinopathic tendons indicated by the microarray, its presence was increased on the protein level. Although we can only speculate on the clearance rate of both soluble and membrane-bound IL-6R as well as of the cells carrying them, the mismatch in its presence on the gene transcription and the protein expression levels could be a legacy from earlier disease stages.
evidence: Based on speculation about temporal dynamics of gene expression and protein accumulation.

claim: IL-6R on CD90+ cells in tendinopathic tendons may have been originally produced by CD68+ cells as part of trans-signaling.
source: Since it has yet to be shown that stromal fibroblasts express and translate IL-6R, a better explanation might be that the IL-6R on CD90+ cells were originally produced by, i.e., the CD68+ cells and ended up on CD90+ cells as part of a trans-signaling process.
evidence: Based on inference from co-localization data and known trans-signaling mechanisms.

claim: The effects of IL-6 on extrinsic fibroblasts in the assembloid model could be dominated by trans-signaling.
source: This indicates that the following described effects of IL-6 on extrinsic fibroblasts could be dominated by trans-signaling.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that IL-6R is present on CD45+ cells from core explants but not on extrinsic fibroblasts.

claim: Recombinant IL-6 rescuing proliferation but not migration suggests the necessity of an IL-6 gradient and/or establishment of a secondary cytokine gradient.
source: Recombinant IL-6 rescuing proliferation but not migration of ScxGFP cells highlights the necessity of an IL-6 gradient and/or the establishment of a secondary cytokine gradient (e.g. TGF-β) by IL-6 (Tan et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and citation to supporting literature.

claim: IL-6 may function as an energy allocator in tendon, accelerating processes like migration by increasing baseline cell metabolism.
source: Alternatively, IL-6 has also been described as an energy allocator in other musculoskeletal tissues and could in this function be accelerating a diverse range of processes (i.e. migration) by increasing the baseline cell metabolism (Kistner et al., 2022).
evidence: Based on inference from literature on IL-6 function in other tissues, with supporting citation.

claim: The upregulation of biological processes related to oxidative stress and hypoxia in extrinsic cells around an IL-6 KO core indicates disrupted energy allocation.
source: Fittingly, the extrinsic cell populations around an IL-6 KO core upregulated biological processes related to oxidative stress and hypoxia, which indicates a disrupted energy allocation.
evidence: Based on inference from GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The ablation of IL-6 might have led to elevation of compensatory IL-6 superfamily ligands or other attractant chemokines/cytokines in vivo.
source: Furthermore, the ablation of IL-6 might have led to the elevation of compensatory IL-6 superfamily ligands (or other attractant chemokines or cytokines) and one can currently only speculate on their in vivo distribution as well as the resulting patterns of fibroblast migration (Dyment et al., 2013; Langberg et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on speculation about potential compensatory mechanisms in IL-6 KO mice, with supporting citations.

claim: The reduced presence of extrinsic fibroblasts in IL-6 KO core explants may result from reduced migration and proliferation.
source: Most of these processes were reduced in an IL-6 KO core, speculatively because of the reduced presence of extrinsic fibroblasts resulting from the reduced migration and proliferation.
evidence: Based on inference connecting RNA-seq results to earlier observations of reduced migration and proliferation.

claim: IL-6 signaling contributes to gene expression behind tendinopathy hallmarks of cellularity and ECM turnover.
source: In contrast to the signatures emerging from the presence of fibroblasts however, the respective contribution of transcripts increased and decreased by the IL-6 KO to the enriched GO biological processes and molecular functions indicates a decreasing cellularity and ECM turnover in the core (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), which could mean that IL-6 signaling contributes to the gene expression behind these tendinopathy hallmarks.
evidence: Based on inference from directional analysis of GO enrichment in IL-6 KO vs WT comparison.

claim: IL-6 signaling accelerates catabolic ECM turnover in tendon core explants.
source: In connection with the bulk RNA-seq data, the changes in the assembloid's ability to resist tension suggest that IL-6 signaling accelerates (catabolic) ECM turnover.
evidence: Based on inference connecting mechanical testing results with RNA-seq data on ECM-related genes.

claim: Decelerated catabolic ECM turnover could be responsible for delayed wound healing in IL-6 KO mice.
source: However, previous studies have already reported a delayed wound healing response in IL-6 KO mice and our experiments here suggest that the decelerated catabolic ECM turnover could be responsible for this (Lin et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on inference connecting current findings to previously published observations, with supporting citation.
